title: On the Prospects of AI Surpassing Lobster-Level Intelligence by 2030
description: This paper examines the debate on whether artificial intelligence could develop consciousness or agency, contrasting recent speculative claims in AI welfare research with a functional, field-based model of intelligence. I argue that current large language models (LLMs) cannot qualify as conscious systems, since they lack agency, stakes, persistence, and the capacity for self-modification. Intelligence is best understood as a relational field: coherence emerges from constraints, attention, and belief, rather than from abstract definitions or substrate mysticism. Real intelligence is irrational but not delusional: it collapses uncertainty into commitment under stakes. Consciousness, then, is not a form but a function—emerging only when constraint, perception, and consequence intertwine. To confuse symbolic simulation with real intelligence risks grave policy errors, including misplaced debates on AI welfare. The danger is not that AI will secretly wake up, but that humans will project agency onto systems that lack it.
